title: A short lecture on urban heat

lines.speaker: Lecturer
lines.text: Today we're looking at a phenomenon called the urban heat island. Simply put, cities are often several degrees warmer than the countryside around them.

lines.speaker: Lecturer
lines.text: There are three main causes. First, materials like concrete and asphalt absorb heat during the day and release it at night. Second, there are fewer trees, so there is less shade. Third, cars and air conditioners produce extra heat.

lines.speaker: Lecturer
lines.text: Why does this matter? Higher temperatures increase energy use and can be dangerous for elderly people.

lines.speaker: Lecturer
lines.text: Fortunately, there are solutions. Planting trees, painting roofs white and creating green spaces can reduce temperatures significantly.

questions.prompt: What is an urban heat island?
options: A hot island near a city
A city that is warmer than the countryside around it

questions.prompt: How many main causes does the lecturer mention?
Which is NOT mentioned as a solution?
Concrete releases heat at night.
questions.explanation: "Absorb heat during the day and release it at night."

title: Learning a language as an adult

lines.text: Today I'm talking to Grace, who learned Spanish at the age of forty. Grace, was it difficult?

lines.speaker: Grace
lines.text: At first, yes. I was worried that it was too late, but actually adults have some advantages: we're more organised and we know why we're learning.

lines.speaker: Host
lines.text: What helped you most?

lines.text: Speaking from the first week. I found a conversation partner online and we talked twice a week, even when I made lots of mistakes.

lines.text: And how long did it take you to feel confident?

lines.speaker: Lecturer
lines.text: Good morning. Today we'll look at why we forget, and what that means for studying.

lines.speaker: Lecturer
lines.text: In the 1880s, the psychologist Hermann Ebbinghaus showed that we forget most new information within a day unless we review it. This is known as the forgetting curve.

lines.speaker: Lecturer
lines.text: However, each time we review something, the curve becomes flatter: we forget more slowly. That's the principle behind spaced repetition — reviewing at increasing intervals, say after one day, then three, then a week.

lines.speaker: Lecturer
lines.text: A second technique is retrieval practice. Testing yourself, rather than simply rereading notes, forces the brain to reconstruct information, which strengthens the memory.

lines.speaker: Lecturer
lines.text: So, for your next exam: little and often, and test yourself.

questions.prompt: What did Ebbinghaus show?
options: We forget most new information within a day without review

questions.prompt: What is spaced repetition?
The lecturer says rereading notes is better than testing yourself.
questions.explanation: Testing yourself (retrieval practice) is more effective.

questions.prompt: What is the lecturer's final advice?
options: Little and often, and test yourself

vocab.def: a graph showing how quickly we forget

lines.speaker: Chair
lines.text: Our motion tonight: university education should be free for all. Dr Adjei, you're in favour.

lines.speaker: Adjei
lines.text: Indeed. Higher education yields benefits far beyond the individual — a healthier, more productive and more engaged citizenry. It seems perverse to price out talented students on the basis of their parents' income.

lines.speaker: Chair
lines.text: Ms Laurent, you oppose the motion.

lines.speaker: Laurent
lines.text: I don't dispute the benefits, but 'free' is a misnomer: someone pays, namely the taxpayer, including those who never attend university. Evidence from several countries suggests that free tuition disproportionately benefits the middle class.

lines.speaker: Adjei
lines.text: That's an argument for targeted grants alongside free tuition, not against free tuition itself.

lines.speaker: Laurent
lines.text: Perhaps, but with finite budgets, I'd rather see money invested in primary schools, where the returns are arguably greater.

lines.speaker: Host
lines.text: Why do we put things off, even when we know it's bad for us?

lines.speaker: Researcher
lines.text: Contrary to popular belief, procrastination isn't primarily a time-management problem. It's an emotion-regulation problem. We delay tasks that make us feel anxious, bored or inadequate, because avoiding them gives us immediate relief.

lines.speaker: Host
lines.text: So better planners won't fix it?

lines.speaker: Researcher
lines.text: Planning helps, but only up to a point. What's far more effective is reducing the emotional cost of starting: break the task into a tiny first step — 'open the document', 'write one sentence' — and be compassionate towards yourself when you slip.

lines.speaker: Host
lines.text: Self-compassion sounds rather soft.

lines.speaker: Researcher
lines.text: It does, but studies show that students who forgave themselves for procrastinating on one exam procrastinated less on the next. Self-criticism, by contrast, tends to feed the cycle.

questions.prompt: According to the researcher, procrastination is mainly…
What does she recommend?
options: A tiny first step and self-compassion

questions.prompt: Students who forgave themselves procrastinated less next time.
What effect does self-criticism tend to have?

vocab.def: to delay doing something
being kind to yourself when you fail
